1886–1969 · United Kingdom

Frederic Bartlett

British psychologist who showed that remembering is reconstructing. With the story 'The War of the Ghosts' he found that memory adapts experience to our cultural schemas.

Biography

Frederic Charles Bartlett was born in 1886 in Stow-on-the-Wold, a small English town. Illness meant he did much of his schooling at home. He studied philosophy in London and later at Cambridge, where he joined the experimental psychology laboratory. During the First World War he ran it while its director was away.

He was the first professor of experimental psychology at the University of Cambridge, from 1931 to 1952, and made the laboratory a leading centre. During the Second World War he researched pilot fatigue and other practical questions, and in 1944 he was behind the creation of the Applied Psychology Unit. He was knighted in 1948 and died in 1969.

Questions he investigated

  • Do we remember what happened or reconstruct it?
  • How does culture influence what we remember?
  • How do people work under fatigue, pressure or complex tasks?

Contributions

Bartlett asked English students to read a Native North American tale, "The War of the Ghosts", and to reproduce it several times over weeks and months. He also used serial reproduction: one person told the story to another, who told it to the next, as in the game of telephone. The stories became shorter, lost their strange details and were transformed to fit what English readers considered logical. Canoes became boats and the supernatural elements disappeared.

From this he concluded that memory is reconstructive: we do not reproduce an exact copy, but rebuild from fragments and from schemas, structures of prior knowledge that organise what we remember. The concept of schema was fundamental to later cognitive psychology.

Collaborations, influences and disagreements

Bartlett broke with the tradition of Hermann Ebbinghaus, who studied memory with nonsense syllables to avoid the influence of meaning. For Bartlett, that meaning was precisely what was interesting. He trained many British psychologists, among them Brenda Milner and Donald Broadbent. His work inspired Elizabeth Loftus's research on false memories.

A documented anecdote

Bartlett wrote that the idea of serial reproduction came from a parlour game popular in the England of his day, in which a message is passed from person to person until it becomes unrecognisable.

Criticism, limits and reception

His methods were loosely controlled: he gave informal instructions and did not analyse his data statistically. In 1999, Erik Bergman and Henry Roediger repeated the study under more rigorous conditions and confirmed that the story is distorted in recall, though less than his examples suggested. His central idea, that remembering is reconstructing, is now one of the pillars of the psychology of memory.

References

  1. Bartlett, F. C. (1932). Remembering: A study in experimental and social psychology. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
  2. Bergman, E. T. y Roediger, H. L. (1999). Can Bartlett's repeated reproduction experiments be replicated? Memory & Cognition, 27(6), 937–947.
  3. Wagoner, B. (2017). The constructive mind: Bartlett's psychology in reference to culture. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
